title: 5 Signs Your Leadership Team Needs Development

# 5 Signs Your Leadership Team Needs Development in the AI Era


Published: 11/19/2026


Table of Contents


- 1. AI Adoption Stops at the Tool Level
- 2. Decisions Are Pushed Onto Senior Leaders
- 3. Teams Aren’t Aligned On What Matters
- 4. Teams Distrust Their Leaders
- 5. Leaders Deliver Results Without Developing Others
- Senior Leaders Own the Development of Their Leadership Team


AI has raised the stakes for every executive team. Senior leaders are expected to translate rapidly evolving technology into clear direction, yet[seven out of 10 employees](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-great-leader-insight-report?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) say AI and technology are outpacing their culture’s ability to adapt.


Closing that gap starts at the top. When senior leaders align on priorities and model decisive behavior, they[set the pace for managers](https://www.franklincovey.com/blog/developing-leaders-in-your-organization/) across the organization. The following five signs reveal where executive teams are falling behind and where targeted development makes the biggest impact.


**Key Takeaways:** ****


- Leadership team development builds the shared behaviors senior leaders use to set priorities and develop the leaders below them.
- Because technology now advances faster than most organizations can keep up with, AI raises the potential cost of underdeveloped leadership teams.
- The clearest signs that leadership development is needed include the spots where decisions stall and few employees are ready to step into leadership roles.


## 1. AI Adoption Stops at the Tool Level


## We can only graduate to leading people through change if we know how to deal with change as humans first.


— Kory Kogon, Vice President of Content Development, FranklinCovey


An organization with an underdeveloped leadership team buys AI tools without explaining the business case behind them and without considering the human component of change. When employees test out the software but the core workflows around them stay the same, adoption slows and ROI isn’t realized.


FranklinCovey research shows that[only 9% of employees](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-ai-transformation-human-imperative?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) say their manager explains to them how AI will help the business grow. That disconnect begins with the executive team, which is responsible for defining where AI fits into the broader strategy and equipping managers to carry the message forward.


Furthermore, FranklinCovey finds that[80% of individual contributors](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-great-leader-insight-report?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) describe their manager’s approach to AI leadership as “hands-off.” That number points to an organizational blind spot: Few executive teams have clearly defined what leading AI adoption actually looks like at each level.


Introducing the tools alone is not enough, no matter how impressive the technology is. Change is always going to be human-led. Senior teams that successfully[lead organizational change](https://www.franklincovey.com/blog/organizational-change/) tie every AI investment to a specific business priority before rollout and know how to help teams navigate the[predictable pattern of change](https://www.franklincovey.com/courses/change/) . Equipped with that context, middle managers can clearly explain the purpose behind every tool to their teams and guide them through each new stage.


**Download our interactive workbook,**[Harnessing AI Disruption](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-harnessing-ai-disruption?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) **, to learn how leaders can turn constant change into organizational momentum that accelerates results.**


## 2. Decisions Are Pushed Onto Senior Leaders


When managers below the executive team lack clear decision rights or the confidence to use them, every choice gets pushed back to the top and execution grinds to a halt.


The data reflects this hesitation: FranklinCovey research reveals that[36% of employees](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-ai-transformation-human-imperative?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) hesitate to make decisions without manager approval. While AI speeds up access to information, human judgment still drives the final call. An organization that routes every choice upward forfeits the very speed AI was meant to create.


Senior leaders reverse this pattern when they[delegate decision rights](https://www.franklincovey.com/courses/6-critical-practices/delegate-to-elevate) with clear guardrails and coach managers through their first independent calls. In an effective handoff, a senior leader sets the budget ceiling and the deadline, then trusts the director to select the vendor without a second review.


## 3. Teams Aren’t Aligned On What Matters


## People are working harder than ever, but because they lack clarity and vision, they aren’t getting very far. They, in essence, are pushing a rope with all of their might.


— Stephen R. Covey


Misalignment at the top compounds at every level beneath it. When executives leave a meeting with competing interpretations of the main priority, each department chases its own version, forcing teams to pause work just to get back on the same page.


FranklinCovey research shows that[92% of employees](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-ai-transformation-human-imperative?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) lose multiple hours each week waiting for clarity or resolving misalignment. Because AI accelerates the sheer volume of change teams must absorb, the cost of ambiguous direction is higher than ever.


Executive teams that commit to[a few high-impact priorities](https://www.franklincovey.com/courses/the-4-disciplines/discipline-1-wildy-important) and review them on a shared weekly cadence give the organization the clarity it needs to move. That rhythm also[fosters accountability across functions](https://www.franklincovey.com/blog/fostering-accountability-in-the-workplace/) . In a disciplined weekly review, each leader reports progress against the same core goals, and the team resolves cross-functional friction before leaving the room.


**Download our guide,**[From Burnout to Breakthrough](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-from-burnout-to-breakthrough?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) **, to learn how leaders create clarity, delegate effectively, and coach talent to drive results and build a stronger leadership pipeline.**


## 4. Teams Distrust Their Leaders


Trust dictates how quickly an executive team’s strategy turns into execution. Employees who trust their leaders typically act with confidence, while employees who doubt their managers either stall or leave. According to recent FranklinCovey data,[only 42% of employees](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-great-leader-insight-report?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) currently view their direct leader as trusted, and two-thirds have low confidence in the overall quality of today’s leaders.


That deficit hits the bottom line directly. A FranklinCovey analysis found that high-trust organizations generate[8.5x more revenue per employee](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-ai-transformation-human-imperative?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) and experience 50% lower turnover. AI only intensifies this pressure, with[nearly half of employees](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-great-leader-insight-report?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) worrying that their roles won’t matter in an AI-driven future.


Strong leadership teams[build trust through consistent behavior](https://www.franklincovey.com/courses/leading-at-the-speed-of-trust/) , honoring commitments, and explaining the rationale behind tough decisions. When a senior leader falls short on a commitment, they must own the miss openly in the next team meeting and set a new target date.


**Download our guide,**[Trust & Inspire®: The Leadership Framework Built for Disruption](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-trust-and-inspire?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) **, to learn how today’s leaders can create confident and engaged teams that drive results during periods of change.**


## 5. Leaders Deliver Results Without Developing Others


An executive team that evaluates managers solely on short-term output creates a fragile bench of leaders who can hit numbers personally, but who aren’t prepared to elevate others. This vulnerability becomes painfully obvious the moment a key role opens up and no internal candidate is ready to step in.


FranklinCovey researchers found that[only 7% of leaders](https://resources.franklincovey.com/c/tlg-great-leader-insight-report?x=j4G37p&lb-mode=overlay) manage to balance both performance expectations and genuine care for their people, which is the exact combination required to sustain results and engagement over time.


Executives close this gap by holding every leader accountable for succession and reviewing talent progress with the same rigor as financial metrics. A formal[leadership development plan](https://www.franklincovey.com/blog/leadership-development-plan/) establishes a clear standard for that work. Leaders who actively coach the potential in their direct reports build a resilient pipeline while delivering today’s results. In a rigorous talent review, each executive identifies one direct report who could step into their role within a year and outlines the exact experience that person still needs to get there.


## Senior Leaders Own the Development of Their Leadership Team


The habits of the senior team set the ceiling for every leader across the enterprise. When development starts in the C-suite, managers at every level gain a working model to follow.


As AI reshapes the workplace, executive teams carry an ongoing responsibility to model the clarity, alignment, and trust they expect their organizations to adopt. That responsibility belongs squarely to the senior leadership team, and it continues long after any single training initiative ends.


Learn what it takes to equip your senior leaders to set the standard for[leadership development](https://www.franklincovey.com/why-franklincovey/leadership/) and lead your organization through ongoing change.
